abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Sleep is fundamental for health and well‐being. An adequate amount and quality of sleep is a cardinal component of a healthy lifestyle at the basis of the prevention of many non‐communicable chronic diseases. Recent evidence suggests that sleep disorders, particularly obstructive sleep apnea, represent an emerging risk factor for periodontal health. This review article provides a critical appraisal of the existing literature concerning the association between sleep duration, sleep quality, sleep disorders in general, and obstructive sleep apnea with periodontal diseases, including gingivitis and periodontitis. The putative mechanisms underlying these associations are described as well as the potential clinical implications for diagnosis and treatment.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Sleep is fundamental for health and well‐being 1 and it is among the health‐related lifestyle factors that need to be addressed to promote the prevention of many non‐communicable chronic diseases, together with nutrition, physical activity, avoidance of tobacco products, and stress management. 2 Indeed, sleep deprivation, circadian misalignment, and untreated sleep disorders are associated with detrimental consequences on physical health, mental health, mood, and public safety. 3 Recent evidence suggests that sleep may also impact oral and periodontal health. 4 Particularly it has emerged over the past decade that sleep disorders may be associated with periodontal conditions with possible implications for clinical diagnosis and management. 4 As part of periodontal medicine, the branch of periodontology that focuses on the research of data establishing the relationship between periodontal health or disease and systemic health or disease, 5 , 6 sleep disorders should be included in the list of different diseases and conditions being associated with periodontal diseases, such as diabetes, 7 atherosclerosis, 8 obesity, 7 respiratory diseases, 9 rheumatoid arthritis, 10 and mortality. 11 Possible explanations of these associations are mainly linked to infection/inflammation pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of many systemic conditions, 12 acting in a unidirectional or potentially bidirectional relationship. 13 The present article aims to summarize the existing literature dealing with sleep and periodontal health. It provides a critical appraisal of the current evidence trying to detail the epidemiological associations, the plausible explanatory mechanisms, and the potential clinical implications. For this purpose, a literature search was conducted on PubMed (Medline), Scopus, and Google Scholar databases using pertinent MeshTerms and keywords related to sleep and periodontal health, without time limits but restricted to studies published in English and dealing with adult populations only. The literature search was conducted in April 2024 and updated on July 10th, 2024. Despite the attempt to be as exhaustive as possible in the description of the available literature, this is a narrative review and the relevance of the articles on which the main sections are based relies upon our own judgment. Finally, a research agenda is proposed to guide future studies in the field.

sec.title: SLEEP PHYSIOLOGY AND SLEEP DISORDERS
The structure of sleep
sec.p: The sleep and wake states differ in various physiological parameters, such as thermoregulation, cardiac activity, metabolism, and respiration. While wake is a state of high metabolic demand, sleep is a state of energy conservation and recovery that contributes to the homeostasis of many physiological and psychological functions. During the 24 h, sleep alternates with wake according to what is called the circadian rhythm, driven and regulated by clock genes which regulate several physiological and behavioral processes. The circadian clock is synchronized to the environment by different cues, including the light/dark cycle (through the central pacemaker located in the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus), 14 , 15 temperature oscillation, stress, and exercise. Social interactions and habits are also important determinants of the synchronization of the wake/sleep alternance. 16 The need of sleep and the propensity to fall asleep increase following extended wakefulness according to a homeostatic process superimposed over the 24 h circadian process. Misalignment of circadian rhythms and sleep can have several adverse health outcomes, including increased risk for all‐cause mortality, obesity, type‐2 diabetes, major depressive disorder, and cardiovascular diseases. 16

A night or a period of sleep is structured into two alternating phases, named REM (from Rapid Eye Movement) and non‐REM (NREM) sleep. Both occur in repeating cycles, with NREM always preceding REM sleep. 17 NREM sleep is further divided into 3 stages, representing light (N1 and N2) and deep (N3) sleep, in which the electroencephalographic (EEG) activity is characterized by the preponderance of high amplitude low‐frequency components (slow wave sleep) and the sleep‐related recovery processes are maximized. On the contrary, REM sleep, also called paradoxical sleep, is characterized by wake‐like EEG activity in the presence of muscle atonia, brought about by the inhibition of motor neurons. This is also the sleep stage most often associated with vivid, intense, and creative dreams. 18 The transition from wakefulness to sleep occurs during N1; sleep onset is defined by the occurrence of N2, to progress toward N3, and then REM sleep. After a period of REM sleep, a brief arousal or full awakening may follow, and this closes the so‐called sleep cycle. A period/night of sleep is composed of 4–6 sleep cycles that last approximately 80–100 min each. The amount of deep sleep is predominant during the first cycles whereas the duration of the REM stage progressively increases across successive sleep cycles. 18 The structure of a period/night of sleep is typically represented in a hypnogram, as displayed in Figure 1.

sec.p: The need of sleep changes across the lifespan, as human wake and sleep patterns are influenced by biological maturation and aging. Newborns will require 14–17 h of sleep per day, 19 in which REM sleep predominates by occupying approximately 50% of their sleep time. With growing, sleep patterns tend to synchronize with feeding and the sleeping schedules of the family environment while the need of sleep progressively decreases, being estimated between 10 and 14 h per day (including napping) for toddlers and pre‐school children. 20 During school age, children need to sleep 9–12 h per 24 h whereas 8–10 h are recommended for teenagers. 19 During adulthood, at least 7 h of sleep per day are recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society, 19 , 21 although sleep duration continues to change according to age and chronotype, with elderly people presenting more fragile and multiphase sleep patterns than mid‐age adults. 21 , 22

sec.title: The roles of sleep
sec.p: Sleep is a complex biological state characterized by behavioral, physiological, and electrophysiological parameters. Approximately, human beings will spend a third of their life sleeping. 22 This gives an idea of the importance of sleep, despite the fact that its multiple roles remain unclear. 23 However, it is known that sleep is essential or substantially contributes to many physiological functions, including the immune system, hormonal systems, thermoregulatory systems, basic metabolic processes, and cognitive function. 22

Sleep duration and sleep quality impact the immune system at the systemic, cellular, and genomic levels. 24 In particular, sleep appears to closely interplay with innate immunity. Monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells, comprising the immune cell types of the innate immune system, serve as the body's first line of defense against tissue damage and microbial infection. 25 In the case of sleep disturbance, an upregulation of the innate immune responses is observed, altering the cascade of inflammatory processes that should help contain an infection and promote healing and recovery. Indeed, an increase in cellular and genomic markers of inflammation is detected, with a sleep‐related production of proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL‐6 and TNF). 24 This may be linked to the presence of reactive oxygen species, nucleotides (e.g., adenosine triphosphate), and heat shock proteins that have accumulated during the wake period and act like classical immunological stimulants. 26 From an epidemiological point of view, insomnia complaints, short sleep duration, and extremely long sleep duration have been associated with higher levels of C‐reactive protein (CRP), 27 linking sleep disturbance to inflammation with effect sizes comparable to those of some demographic (e.g., age and low socioeconomic status) and biobehavioral factors (e.g., sedentary physical activity) known to impact on inflammation. 28 , 29 , 30 On the other hand, a reciprocal relationship may also exist, since inflammatory cytokines homeostatically regulate sleep. 24 , 31 , 32 Thus, because of the interactions between sleep, immunity, and inflammatory mechanisms, it appears clear that managing sleep complaints may contribute to reverse inflammatory disease risk, and potentially, targeting inflammation may help improve sleep. 3 , 24 , 25

An adequate amount and quality of sleep are also essential to preserve metabolic health. Indeed, sleep contributes to glucose regulation, lipid metabolism, appetite‐regulating hormone secretion (e.g., ghrelin and leptin), cortisol, melatonin, and growth hormone release, which are all influenced by the circadian rhythmicity (i.e., the alternance between sleep and wake). 33 , 34

The importance of sleep for cognitive functions is also well known. It is sufficient for a night of sleep loss to observe the immediate and unavoidable consequences on the brain and the various cognitive functions it supports, including fatigue, lack of attention, difficulties in concentration, and mood alterations. 35 These consequences are proportional to the amount of sleep lost and may become detrimental if sleep deprivation becomes chronic (i.e., sleep restriction). Similarly, a very tight link exists between sleep and memory. 36 , 37 , 38 A long time ago it was already observed that memory retention following sleep was superior to retention following an equivalent interval of wake. 39 This was initially explained by the fact that sleep protects newly forming memories from the impact of interfering information. Today, several mechanisms are also investigated at the systemic, synaptic, and molecular levels, involving gene expression, neuronal activity, and plasticity, to explain how sleep promotes long‐term memory consolidation. 35 , 37 , 38

Thus, due to its multiple roles, sleep is an essential lifestyle contributor to health and well‐being, 1 which should be promoted at the general population level as a form of primordial prevention of several chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular diseases and metabolic disorders. 2 , 40 Indeed, sleep has been recently added to the indicators of cardiovascular health, the so‐called Life's Essential 7, which has been updated to Life's Essentials 8 (LE8) in July 2022. 41 Together with a healthy diet, regular physical activity, no exposure to nicotine, healthy weight (body mass index in a normal weight range), blood lipids (non‐HDL cholesterol in a healthy range), blood glucose and blood pressure in a healthy range, and healthy sleep (defined as an average of 7–9 h of sleep per day) correlates with cardiovascular health and a lower risk of cardiovascular diseases. 42 Unfortunately, self‐chosen sleep deprivation is very common in our modern society and the importance of sleep for health, particularly, cardiovascular health remains generally undervalued. 43

sec.title: Sleep disorders
sec.p: Sleep disorders involve problems with the quality, timing, and amount of sleep, which result in distress and impairment in functioning while awake. There are many different types of sleep disorders. The International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD) provides a standardized classification and definitions for sleep disorders. Based on the most recent revision, the ICSD‐III‐TR published in 2023, 44 sleep disorders are classified in the following six major categories: (1) insomnia disorders; (2) sleep‐related breathing disorders (SRBD); (3) central disorders of hypersomnolence; (4) circadian rhythm sleep–wake disorders; (5) parasomnias (e.g., somnambulism and REM behavior disorder); and (6) sleep‐related movement disorders (e.g., sleep bruxism and restless leg syndrome). Sleep disorders affect both children and adults. However, they may present with different signs and symptoms in children than adults. This review focuses exclusively on sleep disorders in adult populations.

Insomnia disorders are the most common among sleep disorders. It is characterized by 3 primary symptoms, such as difficulty falling asleep, difficulty staying asleep, and early morning awakenings that occur at least 3 times a week for at least 3 months. 44 Some individuals may also complain of feeling tired on awakening and it must be considered that insomnia may also be the manifestation of another medical or psychiatric condition. 45

SRBD are very common condition in adults. They include obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), central sleep apnea, sleep‐related hypoventilation disorders, sleep‐related hypoxemia disorder, and isolated symptoms and normal variants, such as snoring. OSA represents one of the most dreadful and prevalent sleep disorders. It is characterized by partial or complete obstruction of the upper airways that leads to episodes of hypopnea or apnea, respectively, during sleep despite the efforts of the respiratory muscles. This is associated with repeated breathing cessation, consequent oxygen desaturations, and repetitive awakenings during sleep, leading to poor quality sleep, excessive daytime sleepiness, and fatigue. 46 , 47

OSA is a complex and heterogeneous disorder, in terms of clinical presentations (e.g., symptoms), etiology, comorbid conditions, and outcomes. 48 It is now widely accepted that OSA is not exclusively linked to the mechanical obstruction of the upper airways due to fat deposits, but multiple mechanisms can explain the collapse of the semi‐rigid pharyngeal structures and the obstructive respiratory events during sleep. These involve muscle responsiveness, the arousal threshold, and the mechanisms linked to the loop gain and critical closing pressure (Pcrit) that determine the degree of collapsibility of the upper airways. 49 Several studies in recent years have characterized OSA patients according to “phenotypes,” which cluster pathophysiologic, molecular, or cellular features that may improve the understanding of the disease mechanisms, predicting the response to therapy, and assessing the risk for adverse events. 50 , 51 Ideally, a phenotype serves as an expression of an “endotype,” a subtype of disease defined by “a unifying and consistent natural history, clinical and physiological characteristics, an underlying pathobiology with identifiable biomarkers and genetics”. 50 To date, OSA patient characterization has well advanced in terms of phenotypes but not yet in terms of endotypes. Still, the phenotyping approach represents a very important step toward the application of personalized medicine and discarding the concept of one disease whose diagnosis and management rely on “one size fits all” criteria. 48

The diagnosis of OSA is based on the clinical criteria listed in the ICSD‐III‐TR together with the objective parameters obtained via a sleep recording (either a full polysomnography [PSG] or a cardio‐respiratory monitoring). 44 The typical OSA signs and symptoms include: snoring, daytime sleepiness, witnessed apneas by the bedpartner, waking up choking or gasping, restless sleep, frequent arousals, nocturia, erectile dysfunction, early morning headaches, lack of energy, poor concentration, fatigue, and mood alterations 47 , 51 , 52 (Box 1). Thanks to a sleep recording (either in a sleep lab or at home), several parameters can be assessed the degree of breathing disorder can be evaluated. The most frequently used metric for OSA is the Apnea Hypopnea Index (AHI) which expresses the number of episodes of apneas and hypopnea per hour of sleep and allows to classify the severity of OSA into mild (AHI: 5–15), moderate (AHI: >15–30), and severe (AHI: >30). 53 Other indexes that can be used are the Respiratory Disturbance Index, the Respiratory Event Index, the arousal intensity, the cardiopulmonary coupling, the desaturation index (SO2), or the sleep time spent with an SO2 < 90% (e.g., hypoxic burden) which may capture different aspects related to OSA and may help in predicting cardiovascular events more than AHI. 53

sec.p: Untreated and severe OSA is associated with several consequences for systemic health, particularly with neurocognitive impairment, hypertension, metabolic disorders, depression, and incident cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events. 47 , 53 , 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 Pooled data analyses indicate that patients with SRBD are 26% more likely to develop cognitive impairment (risk ratio, 1.26; 95% CI: 1.05–1.50), 58 and particularly OSA patients are at increased risk of cardiovascular diseases (odds ratio, 1.71; 95% CI: 1.17–2.27), stroke (odds ratio, 1.86; 95% CI: 1.28–2.69), and cardiovascular disease‐related mortality (odds ratio: 1.77; 95% CI: 1.37–2.29). 59 Moreover, OSA significantly increased the risk of motor vehicle crashes (mean crash‐rate ratio ranging from 1.21 to 4.89) 60 and occupational injuries through the impact of sleep fragmentation on vigilance and reaction time. 60 , 61 , 62

sec.title: Epidemiology of sleep disorders
sec.p: Sleep deprivation and sleep disorders are highly prevalent in the general adult population, with approximately one‐third experiencing trouble sleeping at some point during their lifetime. 63 Based on data from the 2005 to 2008 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 13.8% of adults in the United States report a sleep duration <6 h per day and 23.1% between 6 and 7 h, 64 which is most of the times considered as an insufficient amount of sleep. 19 , 21 Consistently, data from the 2014 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System on 444 306 adults showed that only 65.2% of respondents reported a healthy sleep duration (≥7 h), with significant variations related to geographical and ethnical origins. 65

In Europe, data from the Survey of Health Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), a cross‐national study conducted on a representative sample of 54 722 non‐institutionalized adults aged ≥50 years, showed that 24.2% of respondents have suffered from sleep disorders in the previous 6 months. 66 The prevalence rates differed among European countries, ranging from 16.6% in Denmark and Italy to 31.2% in Poland. 66 In general, the prevalence of sleep disorders is higher among women than men.

Concerning specific sleep disorders, insomnia disorder is the most common sleep disorder. It likely affects 5%–15% of the US population, with approximately 30% reporting significant symptoms at any given time, 67 and another 20% experiencing occasional insomnia symptoms. 45 Women, older adults, and people with low income and educational levels are more vulnerable to insomnia. Due to its high prevalence and high persistence rate over a 5‐year period (40%), insomnia is a chronic disease associated with a great public health burden. 45 , 68

Concerning OSA, the most harmful sleep disorder, it is estimated that nearly one billion people aged between 30 and 69 are affected worldwide, with a prevalence above 50% in some of the 16 countries with reliable prevalence, such as China, United States, Brazil, and India (based on an AHI* ≥5 per hour of sleep). 69 In the United States, approximately 31% of men and 17% of women aged between 30 and 70 years are affected by a form of OSA, with a global increase in the prevalence rate due to the concomitant increased rate of obesity, which remains one of the major risk factors for OSA. 70

Epidemiological data also suggest that OSA may be more prevalent among individuals of minority backgrounds, 71 , 72 , 73 obese patients, 74 , 75 men, 76 and patients with comorbidities. 77 , 78 In a population‐based study conducted in Lausanne, Switzerland (HypnoLaus), investigating 2121 adult individuals, the prevalence of moderate‐to‐severe SRBD (≥15 events per h) was estimated at 23.4% (95% CI: 20.9%–26.0%) in women and 49.7% (95% CI: 46.6%–52.8%) in men. The authors also observed that higher AHI was independently associated with the presence of hypertension, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and depression. 77 Based on self‐reported data gathered via the Berlin Questionnaire in the population‐based cohort CONSTANCES, the weighted prevalence of treated sleep apnea or high risk of OSA was estimated at 20.9% (95% CI: 20.0%–21.9%) in France. 79 Finally, OSA has a non‐negligible impact in terms of healthcare expenses related to working days being lost, productivity loss, associated comorbidity costs, and workplace or motor vehicle accident risk that adds to the disease's economic impact. 52 , 69 , 80 However, most of OSA cases remain undiagnosed, likely due to an asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic state, and the fact the early signs and symptoms may be disregarded or underestimated by the patient and physician(s). 81

Together these data indicate that sleep disorders are a major public health problem, 66 which needs to be addressed at the population level to raise public awareness and education about sleep health, and, consequently, try to decrease their incidence and related disease burdens. 82

sec.title: IMPACT OF SLEEP DISORDERS ON GENERAL HEALTH
sec.p: Sleep is generally perceived by our society as a nonproductive state and, unfortunately, its importance for health is often neglected. The tendency to increase wake time over sleep is quite common and dictated by environmental, social, and behavioral decisions; however, this paradoxically reduces performance and leads to poorer general health. 1

As deemed by the numerous roles of sleep, insufficient sleep, and sleep disorders are linked to several medical consequences, such as cognitive impairment, increased likelihood of motor vehicle and other transportation accidents, industrial accidents, medical errors, and loss of work productivity. Sleep disorders also increase the risk of hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, obesity, diabetes, metabolic disorders, cancer, and mortality. 15 , 40 , 56 , 74 , 83 Finally, in the last years, evidence has also emerged for a bidirectional relationship between sleep and neurodegenerative disorders. 84 Indeed, sleep disorders can represent an independent risk factor for neurodegeneration and may exacerbate neuropathology in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's Disease, and other neurodegenerative disorders, subsequently influencing their course and outcome. 84

sec.title: EPIDEMIOLOGICAL EVIDENCE OF THE ASSOCIATION BETWEEN SLEEP DISORDERS AND PERIODONTAL DISEASES
sec.p: Recent data suggest that sleep quality, sleep duration, and the presence of sleep disorders have an impact on periodontal health and diseases. From an anatomical perspective, the periodontium comprises the tooth‐supporting tissues that surround the teeth, including the cementum, the periodontal ligament, the alveolar bone, and the gingiva, which anchor them in the jaws through the periodontal attachment. From a clinical standpoint, periodontal health is defined as a condition free from periodontal pathology (objectivized by a bleeding on probing score < 10% and no pocket deeper than 3–4 mm), pain, and edema in a pristine periodontium or reduced periodontium. 85 Periodontal diseases, as a general term for pathologies of the periodontium, that is, gingivitis or periodontitis, are inflammatory diseases of the periodontium, which are initiated by the accumulation of the bacterial plaque. 86 In the presence of a dysbiotic bacterial biofilm, the host inflammatory responses are triggered; they can be restricted to the gingival tissues (i.e., gingivitis) or extend to the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone (i.e., periodontitis). Periodontitis is responsible for the loss of the tooth attachment, which creates a pocket between the root surface and the gingiva, and thus constitutes a reservoir for periodontal pathogens. The deepening of periodontal pockets causes further alveolar bone loss, tooth mobility, and eventually tooth loss if periodontitis is left untreated. 87 Periodontitis is a very frequent non‐communicable chronic inflammatory disease. As defined by the CPITN† class IV,‡ periodontitis ranks 7th and 32nd globally for prevalence and incidence, with 1.09 billion (0.828–1.36) prevalent and 91.5 million (74.2–110) incident cases in 2019. 88 The highest prevalence is observed between the age of 55 and 59 years, whereas the pick of incidence is observed around the age of 38 years. 89

It is thus of interest to explore the potential link between sleep disorders and periodontal diseases, as both are prevalent conditions affecting the same patient population. Considering the consequences of chronic and untreated sleep disorders on the metabolic, endocrine, immune, and inflammatory systems, a relationship between sleep and periodontal diseases (gingivitis and periodontitis) is biologically plausible, clinically relevant, and worth studying. Hereafter, we summarized the current evidence focusing on sleep quality, sleep duration, sleep disorders, and in particular OSA, with periodontal health and diseases.

sec.title: Sleep quality and oral/periodontal health
sec.p: Despite a lack of consensus, 90 sleep quality is defined as an individual's self‐satisfaction with the sleep experience, integrating aspects of sleep efficiency (i.e., the ratio of the amount of total time asleep versus the total time in bed), sleep latency (i.e., the transition time from the state of wakefulness to sleep), sleep quantity (i.e., the total amount of hours of sleep across the 24 h period), and wake after sleep onset (i.e., total amount of wake time after sleep onset until final awakening). 91 Measuring sleep quality is challenging due to its subjective nature and unstandardized definition. 90 Nevertheless, assessment of sleep quality is routinely done through the use of diary‐based measures, subjective and objective sleep parameters, and self‐report questionnaires. In particular, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) is a widely used, 18‐item instrument that allows to evaluate sleep quality via seven components: sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, sleeping medication use, and daytime dysfunction. 92 The final PSQI score has been shown to accurately characterize sleep quality, with a PSQI >5 identifying individuals with poor sleep quality.

Table 1 summarizes the literature concerning the association between sleep quality and periodontal health. It includes 6 cross‐sectional studies 93 , 94 , 95 , 96 , 97 , 98 and 1 case–control study. 99 The majority of the studies (5 out of 7) are consistent in observing that poor sleep quality is associated with an increased odd of periodontitis. In particular, Marruganti et al. 93 found, in the convenient sample of 235 adults seeking dental treatment, that individuals with poor sleep quality have a 3‐fold increased risk of presenting with Stage III/IV periodontitis than individuals with good sleep quality (OR: 3.0; 95% CI: 1.2–7.4). Similar results were reported by other cross‐sectional studies, observing a significant association between the PSQI score and the severity of periodontitis. This relationship is also corroborated by the case–control study of Singh et al. 99 (n = 200), which shows an adjusted OR of 3.04 (95% CI: 1.42–6.50). Conversely, Safak et al. 94 as well as Islam et al. 96 did not find an association between the PSQI and the community periodontal index (CPI). These authors are the only ones to use the CPI among the studies cited to screen for periodontal disease. This suggests that the CPI may not be able to capture the relationship between sleep quality and periodontal health, as it represents a basic assessment of periodontal health. 100

sec.title: Sleep duration and sleep disorders and oral/periodontal health
sec.p: Several studies demonstrated the presence of a U‐shaped association between sleep duration and poorer health, indicating that individuals with both insufficient and excessive sleep duration have a greater risk, compared to those with adequate sleep duration (6–8 h), of cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, obesity, cancer, cognitive disorders, depression, and mortality. 83 , 101 , 102 Similarly, the current literature suggests that sleep duration impacts periodontal health, being associated with increased odds of periodontal diseases, particularly periodontitis 103 (Figure 2). We identified 18 relevant articles, which included 16 cross‐sectional studies, 96 , 104 , 105 , 106 , 107 , 108 , 109 , 110 , 111 , 112 , 113 , 114 , 115 , 116 , 117 , 118 , 119 1 case–control study, 109 and 1 retrospective cohort study 120 (Table 2). Among these studies, periodontal assessment was based on various methods, including the CDC/AAP definition (six studies), the CPI (six studies), self‐reported data (two studies), and clinical data typically used for diagnosing periodontal diseases (two studies).

sec.p: Sleep duration was not significantly associated with periodontitis in four cross‐sectional studies. 96 , 106 , 111 , 118 Conversely, 14 other studies have shown an association between periodontitis and sleep duration. To summarize, these studies indicate that people with sleep disorders have a higher prevalence of periodontal diseases compared to those without sleep disorders. Additionally, sleeping less than 5–6 h or more than 8–9 h increases the risk of periodontitis. 116 This is consistent with the U‐shaped risk model (Figure 2), which shows that insufficient sleep and excessive sleep time are associated with a higher risk of comorbidities related to sleep disorders. 101 , 102 Two studies suggest that diabetes may strengthen the relationship between sleep and periodontitis. 112 , 113 Altered sleep duration and sleep patterns can also be considered as a proxy of sleep disorders in general. Few studies have investigated the association between sleep disorders and periodontal health. In a population‐based cross‐sectional survey conducted in France, adults who reported chronically suffering from sleep disorders (other than OSA) were found to be 1.2 times more likely to display severe gingival inflammation. 115 Similarly, in Korea, adults with sleep disorders presented with a 36% higher incidence of severe periodontitis compared to good sleepers. 120 These are also the conclusions of a recent systematic review on the topic, including 13 studies from 10 different countries (comprising >200 000 participants). 103 Moreover, when assessing the role of the LE8 metrics (including sleep duration) developed for cardiovascular health, recent studies analyzing the NHANES 2009–2014 data, showed a lower prevalence of periodontitis among individuals with a higher score of LE8, suggesting that sleep, as part of the healthy lifestyle‐related factors and behaviors, contributes to periodontal health. 121 , 122 , 123

sec.title: Obstructive sleep apnea and oral/periodontal health
sec.p: OSA is a sleep disorder more often investigated in relation to oral and periodontal health. The present review retrieves 25 articles, including 7 case–control 124 , 125 , 126 , 127 , 128 , 129 and 18 cross‐sectional studies 128 , 130 , 131 , 132 , 133 , 134 , 135 , 136 , 137 , 138 , 139 , 140 , 141 , 142 , 143 , 144 , 145 , 146 , 147 , 148 (Table 3). The first study was published in 2009 by Gunaratnam et al., 143 who observed in a convenient sample of 66 OSA patients seen in a sleep center in Australia that the prevalence of periodontitis was 4 times higher than that reported in the national survey. The authors also found that CAL was significantly associated with the total sleep time and they were probably the first group of researchers to suggest an association between OSA and periodontitis. Since then, several epidemiological and clinical studies conducted in different countries (e.g., Korea, Taiwan, the United States, Turkey, Brazil, Colombia, Spain, India, Israel, and China) confirmed that the prevalence of periodontitis is significantly higher in OSA patients than non‐OSA patients. Recent meta‐analyses assessing the relationship between OSA and periodontitis showed an association between OSA and the incidence rate of periodontitis (OR: 0.52; 95% CI: 0.49–0.55; I 2: 98.43%; p = 0.000; n = 43 414) 149 and an increased odds of severe periodontitis in SRBD patients (OR: 1.39; 95% CI: 1.20–1.61; I 2: 0%; p = 0.000; n = 43 296). 150 In general, OSA has been found independently associated with periodontitis with odds ratios ranging from 1.2 to 4.1. 149 , 150 , 151 This association appears to be independent of tooth loss and other established risk factors for periodontitis, including age, male sex, smoking, diabetes, and obesity, on which the statistical analyses were adjusted in most of the studies. A potential “dose‐effect” relationship was also suggested, observing a worsening of the mean depth of the periodontal pocket with an increase in OSA severity, especially in adults up to the age of 50 years. 129 , 144 , 147 Few studies also suggested a bidirectional relationship, with a prevalence of OSA significantly higher in periodontitis patients than in non‐periodontitis patients. 129 , 131 , 147 The only longitudinal propensity‐score‐matched‐case–control study published so far observed that the probability of disease‐free status was significantly lower in the OSA group than in the non‐OSA group, meaning that OSA patients have an increased risk of developing periodontitis over a mean follow‐up of 5 years. 131 Conversely, six studies were not able to confirm a significant association between OSA and periodontitis. 124 , 126 , 139 , 140 , 142 , 145 These studies were conducted on smaller samples of patients ranging from 50 to 260 adults.

sec.title: SLEEP AND PERIODONTITIS: THE PUTATIVE BIOLOGICAL LINKS
sec.p: It remains unknown whether a “cause‐effect” relationship exists between sleep disorders and periodontitis, or whether we are just facing a phenomenon of intersection prevalence between two common chronic diseases sharing multiple risk factors, consequences, and comorbidities. 4 , 152 However, few hypotheses could be advanced to explain how sleep, and particularly OSA, may be considered as an emergent risk indicator for periodontal disease development and progression.

One possible explanatory mechanism involves innate immunity and inflammatory processes, which are finely regulated by sleep. 24 Indeed, sleep loss and sleep disorders induce the activation of vascular endothelial markers (e.g., E‐selectin and s‐ICAM‐1), inflammatory gene expression, and pro‐inflammatory cytokines production (e.g., IL‐1, IL‐6, and TNF‐α). 153 Chronic sleep disorders can significantly impair immune cell function and diminish response to infection, resulting in exacerbated tissue damage face to periodontal pathogens. An experimental animal study showed that sleep‐deprived rats display greater gingival inflammation and more rapid alveolar bone loss than non‐sleep‐deprived rats, supporting the role of sleep disorders and fatigue as a potential risk factors for periodontitis. 154 In humans, it is hard to identify inflammatory markers specifically linked to OSA and/or periodontitis. However, IL‐1b was found to be significantly higher in the gingival crevicular fluid of OSA patients than in controls and it was significantly correlated with periodontal clinical parameters. 127 Conversely, no significant difference was found for TNF‐α and hs‐CRP levels (both in serum, saliva, and gingival crevicular fluid). 127 , 144 , 146 Oxidative stress and impaired antioxidant defense systems may also play a major role, being related to both OSA and periodontitis and their associated comorbidities (e.g. obesity and cardiovascular diseases). 155 Altered sleep patterns are associated with lower levels of melatonin, a free‐radical scavenger effective against oxidative damage, which may also have an anti‐inflammatory role. Thus, low expression of melatonin is associated with an increase in proinflammatory cytokines, like IL‐1β, and TNF‐α that may be harmful for periodontal health. 156

In the specific case of OSA, intermittent hypoxia and repetitive sleep arousals are associated with low‐grade systemic inflammation, insulin resistance, glucose intolerance, hormonal disruption, and increased activity of the sympathetic nervous system, resulting, if left untreated, in many severe health consequences described above (e.g., diabetes, endothelial dysfunction, and hypertension). 157 In this scenario, periodontal breakdown may be as well exacerbated by the presence of OSA.

Alternatively, it can be hypothesized that OSA, through prolonged mouth breathing, snoring, and intermittent hypoxia, may impact upon bacterial colonization of the oral cavity and influence the oral microbiota composition that may shift from a host–microbiota symbiosis to a dysbiosis, at the basis of periodontitis development. 158 Although this hypothesis remains basically unexplored, some data suggest that sleep may interfere with the oral microbiota composition also in healthy individuals, being salivary Prevotella and Corynebacterium in higher relative abundance upon awakening than before sleep. 159 In severe OSA patients, the amount of periodontal pathogens in the dental biofilm appeared to be higher compared to mild/moderate OSA or control individuals, 160 and they also tend to present with higher plaque accumulation and higher prevalence of Prevotella sp., a known periodontal pathogen. 161 Finally, the role of lifestyle, behaviors, addictions, and socioeconomic factors must be taken into consideration when interpreting studies assessing the association between OSA and periodontitis, which is complex and multifactorial (Figures 3 and 4).

sec.title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN TOOTH LOSS AND SLEEP DISORDERS
sec.p: The literature also suggests a relationship between tooth loss and sleep disorders (Table 4). On one side, tooth loss can be considered as a proxy of periodontitis, begin this latter disease the leading cause of tooth loss in adulthood. 162 Thus, it would be expected that individuals with poor sleep quality and sleep disorders (exposure) are more likely to have missing teeth due to poorer oral and periodontal health (outcome). However, it has also been suggested that tooth loss may be associated with morphological changes in the orofacial region together with altered neuromuscular control of the oropharyngeal area that may negatively impact the permeability of the upper airways and predispose to SRBD. 163 In particular, following complete edentulism, anatomical changes involve hard, soft, and muscular tissues, with a marked resorption of the alveolar bones, a reduction in the vertical dimension, a mandibular rotation, and a more retracted resting position of the tongue. 163 , 164 These changes contribute to impaired upper airway size and function and may contribute to an increase in the risk of SRBD and OSA. 165 , 166 In this latter hypothesis, tooth loss (thus partial and complete edentulism) represents the exposure and SRBD the outcome. The current evidence indeed supports both hypotheses.

sec.p: Based on an epidemiological study conducted on a representative sample of the US population aged between 25 and 65 years, the risk of OSA (assessed as the number of suggestive signs and symptoms) increases by 2% for each tooth being lost. 167 A direct proportionality was found between the number of missing teeth and the risk of OSA: the risk of OSA is 25% higher in individuals with 5–8 missing teeth than individuals with 0–4 missing teeth and it increases at 36% when more than 8 teeth are missing. Complete edentulism is associated with a 61% greater risk of OSA. Moreover, retaining a higher number of posterior occlusal contacts was found to be protective against OSA. 167 More recent studies confirmed this association, reporting a more severe OSA in edentulous individuals compared to age‐, gender‐, and BMI‐matched, dentate individuals 168 , 169 , 170 and depending on the time since edentulism. 168 A significant association was also found between the number of remaining natural teeth and the quality and duration of sleep. 170 , 171 , 172 A U‐shaped pattern has been described also in this case, 104 showing that both insufficient sleep and excessive sleep time are associated with a higher likelihood of missing teeth. Also, individuals sleeping <5 h were found to be at increased risk of having <25 natural remaining teeth 172 and completely edentulous individuals were found to be at 59% increased risk of deficient sleep. 171

The impact of edentulism and its prosthetic rehabilitation with partial or complete dentures has been the subject of several studies. 173 Early publications suggested that in edentulous patients with OSA, sleeping with dentures may contribute to reducing the number of apnea/hypopnea episodes per hour of sleep thanks to a relevant increase in the retropharyngeal space, as measured by cephalometry, which translates into improved airway permeability during sleep. 165 Conversely, randomized clinical trials conducted in untreated OSA patients showed that wearing or not a complete denture during sleep does not significantly modify the AHI, leaving it to the experience and practice of the dentist to advise the patient on what to do during sleep. 173 , 174 , 175

However, when research deals with tooth loss, it is very important to understand that is not exclusively the number of missing teeth that matters but also the residual masticatory capacity linked to the number of functional masticatory units (i.e., pairs of occluding premolars and molars) and whether an adequate prosthetic rehabilitation is realized or not. The threshold of 5 functional masticatory units (FMU) has been used in multiple studies to define a sufficient or insufficient number of FMUs, 11 , 115 , 176 , 177 considering the WHO recommendation that indicates that throughout life, the retention of a minimum of 20 teeth is necessary for adequate masticatory efficiency and ability. 178 Thus, whenever missing teeth are not replaced and the number of FMU is insufficient, masticatory impairment and disability may lead to altered nutritional habits, favor imbalanced dietary intake (e.g., ultra‐processed food), predispose to digestive and metabolic diseases, and lower quality of life. 179 , 180 , 181 Thus, a vicious cycle may be established, linking poor sleep and OSA to periodontitis through tooth loss, impaired masticatory function, and related diseases (Figure 4). Finally, the role of socioeconomic status, access to care, lifestyle, and behavioral components (e.g., smoking), must be always taken into consideration as mediators of confounders in the association between sleep and tooth loss, which requires further investigations.

sec.title: ASSOCIATION VERSUS CAUSATION: THE EXAMPLE OF SLEEP DISORDERS
sec.p: Evidence suggests that poor sleep, inadequate amount of sleep, and sleep disorders have an impact on general health and may also contribute to poor oral health, particularly on periodontitis (Figure 5). Based on the available literature, we can only establish associations between these conditions. A statistical association between two variables does not necessarily imply that one causes the other. To claim that an association represents a causal effect, confounding and collider bias need to be ruled.

caption.p: Sleep, general health, and oral/periodontal health. As sleep is essential for general health and it is a cardinal target of health prevention strategies (e.g., Life's Essential 8), it should be considered also when assessing oral and periodontal health, for both prevention and treatment purposes.

sec.title: Is there a causal link between sleep disorders and periodontitis?
sec.p: The interplay between sleep disorders and periodontitis, in the context of other associated general conditions (third variables), is complex and requires further research. It is of interest to consider causal inference with simple directed acyclic graphs (Figures 6, 7, 8), introducing the concepts of confounding, common cause, collider, common effect, and indirect causal pathways (i.e., mediation) to better understand this complexity. Readers can learn more about causal inference in the article by Lederer et al. 182

caption.p: What is the role of poor general health in the relationship between sleep disorders (exposure) and periodontitis (outcome)? Each arrow represents a causal effect. The horizontal arrow represents a direct causal path. The A, B, and C figures correspond to the different models possibly explaining the association between periodontitis and sleep disorders, taking into account the role of poor general health as a confounder (A), collider (B), or mediator (C).

sec.title: Do sleep disorders contribute to periodontitis in patients with poor overall health?
sec.p: Indeed, the relationship between sleep disorders (exposure) and periodontitis (outcome) raises the question of the role of poor general health (Figure 6). For instance, obesity increases the risk of both OSA and periodontitis. 76 , 183 Therefore, obesity should be considered a confounding factor (Figure 6A) and must be included as an adjustment variable in predictive models. Other diseases, such as diabetes, are common to both disorders and should also be adjusted for. 184 , 185 However, it is widely accepted that both sleep disorders and periodontitis have a negative effect on general health. This has been demonstrated in their relationship with cardiovascular disease, supporting the hypothesis that poor general health is a common effect of sleep disorders and periodontitis. 56 , 186 , 187 If this hypothesis is true, poor general health is a collider, and no adjustments should be made (Figure 6B). It also is possible that the relationship between sleep disorders and periodontitis is mediated by poor general health (Figure 6C). For instance, OSA can increase the risk of diabetes by disrupting glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity, which in turn can increase the risk of periodontitis. If poor general health is the mechanism that transmits the effect of sleep disorders to periodontitis, no adjustments should be made.

sec.title: Do periodontitis contribute to sleep disorders in patients with poor overall health?
sec.p: Currently, there is no evidence of the impact of periodontitis on sleep disorders development or progression. However, it is important to note that association studies do not indicate the direction of the association. Therefore, it cannot be ruled out; we cannot exclude that periodontitis could contribute to poor sleep or sleep disorders. Nevertheless, reversing the exposure (periodontitis) and outcome (sleep disorders) would not alter the above comments.

sec.title: Do periodontitis contribute to poor overall health in patients with sleep disorders?
sec.p: Periodontitis have been associated with numerous diseases, and there is no doubt that periodontitis contributes to poor overall health 12 , 188 (Figure 7). Based on the present literature review, it seems that sleep disorders, in particular OSA, maybe a confounder in the relationship between periodontitis (exposure) and overall health (outcome) (Figure 7A). Therefore, models predicting systemic disease resulting from periodontal status should adjust for the sleep disorder variable. However, it is important to note that periodontitis and certain diseases, such as respiratory diseases, could also cause OSA, which would not require adjustment as it is a collider (Figure 7B). The hypothesis that sleep disorders, specifically OSA, mediates the association between periodontitis and poor general health can be ruled out (Figure 7C). There is no evidence to suggest that OSA is a necessary factor in this association.

caption.p: What is the role of sleep disorders in the relationship between periodontitis (exposure) and poor general health (outcome)? Each arrow represents a causal effect. The horizontal arrow represents a direct causal path. The A, B, and C figures correspond to the different models possibly explaining the association between periodontitis and poor general health, taking into account the role of sleep disorders as a confounder (A), collider (B), or mediator (C).

sec.title: Do poor overall health contribute to periodontitis in patients with sleep disorders?
sec.p: Research has shown a bidirectional relationship between poor general health and periodontitis, especially in cases of diabetes. 184 If the direction of the causal link is reversed, with poor overall health becoming the exposure and periodontitis becoming the result, the above comments remain valid, particularly with regard to diabetes and obesity.

sec.title: Do sleep disorders contribute to poor overall health in patients with periodontitis?
sec.p: Numerous studies have shown the negative impact of sleep disorders on general health. 1 Periodontitis can contribute to exacerbate sleep disorders, for example through obesity or respiratory disease, thus contributing to systemic inflammation (Figure 8). A bidirectional relationship between periodontitis and sleep disorders cannot therefore be ruled out. According to this hypothesis, periodontitis would act as a confounding factor between sleep disorders and poor general health (Figure 8A). Consequently, the association between sleep disorders and poor general health should be adjusted for periodontitis. On the other hand, if periodontitis is a collider (Figure 8B), which cannot be discarded, using it as an adjustment variable would be a mistake. Finally, there is no evidence nowadays that periodontitis is a necessary part of the process linking sleep disorders to poor general health. The mediating role of periodontitis in the relationship between these conditions can be excluded (Figure 8C).

The horizontal arrow represents a direct causal path. The A, B, and C figures correspond to the different models possibly explaining the association between sleep disorders and poor general health, taking into account the role of periodontitis as a confounder (A), collider (B), or mediator (C).

sec.title: Do poor overall health contribute to sleep disorders in patients with periodontitis?
sec.p: The previous observations remain unchanged even if we reverse the direction of the causal effect, making poor general health exposure and sleep disorders the result.

In conclusion, when considering the relationship between periodontitis and sleep disorders, it is important to take into account associated comorbidities. For instance, the link between OSA and obesity is not as strong as that between periodontitis and OSA, and the systemic impact of periodontitis differs from that of OSA. Studying a potential causal link, however, can help us understand the complexity of this association, according to its direction and the role of each player.

sec.title: CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS OF THE ASSOCIATION BETWEEN SLEEP DISORDERS AND PERIODONTITIS
sec.p: To date, evidence is lacking to establish a causal relationship between sleep disorders or OSA and periodontitis. However, it appears that the association between these diseases is frequent at the population level and clinicians may encounter patients affected by sleep disorders and periodontitis. In these cases, specific clinical considerations are required to perform an appropriate screening and diagnostic process, to characterize the risk profile of the patient, to consider the potential impact of the comorbidity, and to personalize the management strategy.

sec.title: Screening and diagnosis
sec.p: Although the diagnosis of sleep disorders is the responsibility of a physician, dentists have an important role in the screening process. According to the epidemiological evidence summarized above, it is important to screen for sleep disorders in patients with periodontal diseases and vice versa, meaning screening for oral and periodontal diseases in patients seeking medical advice and treatments for sleep disorders, particularly OSA. In this context, it is desirable to establish a close collaboration with sleep specialists to have a multidisciplinary approach to sleep disorders.

To screen for sleep disorders, several self‐administered questionnaires have been developed and validated. 189 For instance, the Pittsburg Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) for overall sleep quality, the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) for excessive daytime sleepiness, the Berlin questionnaire or the No‐SAS and STOP‐BANG for OSA risk assessment. 76 , 190 , 191 , 192 , 193 Moreover, dentists are well placed to observe the typical signs and symptoms of disrupted sleep and OSA, such as macroglossia, micrognathia, hypertrophic tonsils, mouth breathing, overweight and obesity, excessive sleepiness, and fatigue. Similarly, physicians must refer the patients for a dental and periodontal visit in case of diagnosis of sleep disorders and particularly if a mandibular advancement device is indicated for OSA management.

Moreover, clinicians must keep in mind the potential synergic effect of this association. 115 For instance, OSA is a recognized risk factor for cardiovascular health, 56 , 194 , 195 and severe periodontitis has been linked to several cardiovascular diseases. 8 Both conditions have been linked to endothelial dysfunction, 196 , 197 a predisposing condition for cardiovascular disease development that could be improved by treating OSA and periodontitis. 198 , 199 , 200 , 201 Moreover, the inflammatory nature of these diseases and their association may further contribute to the risk of cardiovascular events over time. Unfortunately, the impact of the comorbidity has not yet been evaluated in clinical studies, but it is relevant for physicians in the characterization of the patient's risk profile and in the decision‐making process leading to the most appropriate disease management. 4

sec.title: Considerations for treatment
sec.p: As said, dentists have an important role in the screening process for sleep disorders and OSA. Moreover, dentists may be involved in the management of OSA, particularly when OSA can be treated by a mandibular advancement device (MAD). MAD refers to a custom‐made or thermoplastic, dual‐bloc, adjustable oral appliance to be worn during sleep to maintain the mandible in an advanced position, together with the tongue base, and enlarge the pharyngeal airway space. MADs are considered for the treatment of mild‐to‐moderate OSA, and they have been proven effective in reducing the AHI and improve OSA‐related signs (e.g., snoring) and symptoms (e.g., sleepiness). 202 , 203 Moreover, MADs represent a treatment option for severe OSA patients in case of refusal or non‐tolerance of non‐invasive ventilation treatments, namely by continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), 204 , 205 , 206 which remains the gold standard for OSA management. 205 , 207 , 208

An optimal oral, dental, and periodontal health is a pre‐requirement for MAD use. 209 , 210 This means the absence of untreated dental caries, periodontal diseases, oral infections, and orofacial pain. Thus, a comprehensive dental and periodontal assessment is necessary to diagnose oral and periodontal health 85 , 211 and rule out possible clinical findings that may preclude the use of MAD. The presence of untreated severe periodontitis may represent a contraindication to MAD due to gingival inflammation, tooth mobility, and reduced periodontal support. 212 In this case, MAD can be considered only after periodontal treatments and when periodontal stability has been reached. Then, MAD effectiveness and safety must be regularly monitored to verify the adaptation of the device and its impact on the teeth and periodontal tissues.

MAD effectiveness is strictly dependent on the adaptation of the device, the compliance of the patient, and its long‐term use. 48 , 213 , 214 , 215 Young, non‐obese, female, patients with an AHI < 30 and specific craniofacial morphology (e.g., retrognathia), seem to be the best candidates for MAA treatment. 204 , 215 , 216 However, the long‐term use of MAD has been associated with the occurrence of side effects, mainly linked to dental and skeletal changes. 217 The most frequent are occlusal changes, including upper incisor retroclination, lower incisor proclination, decreased overjet and overbite, and changes in the total occlusal contact area. 218 Interestingly, no periodontal side effect has been reported in the literature, and the only study assessing periodontal parameters of 21 OSA patients followed‐up for an average of 8 years, observed no significant changes in probing pocket depth, recession, and clinical attachment level under MAD treatment. 219 However, it must be noted that all patients were periodontally healthy at baseline, and no conclusion can be drawn about MAD‐related effects in case of reduced periodontium or history of periodontitis, since in the majority of the cases, these represented an exclusion criterion in randomized clinical trials on the use of MAD for OSA. 218 Still, few studies applying a finite element analysis suggest that the impact of MAD on the periodontium is strictly related to the MAD design and titration system, with some geometries exerting more incremental stress on the periodontal tissues than others. 220 , 221 Moreover, higher stress values are expected in the case of alveolar bone resorption due to the loss of periodontal ligament surface, making the choice of the MAD type and design cardinal in case of reduced periodontium or history of periodontitis. 222 , 223 , 224

It can be hypothesized that MAD use could disrupt the homeostasis of the oral cavity and lead to temporary and/or long‐lasting changes, such as dry mouth or excessive salivation that may also impact the oral microbiota composition. 225 To date, this aspect remains unclear, but it is clinically evident that patients treated by MAD require specific and long‐term follow‐up to periodically check oral and periodontal health. This is also recommended for patients treated by CPAP, which may directly influence the dryness of the oral cavity, the plaque accumulation, and the gingival inflammation. Literature is scarce on the topic and controversial results have been published. For instance, Tsuda et al. investigated oral health in a sample of 744 CPAP users and observed that almost 40% of them complained of oral symptoms. In particular, OSA patients with diabetes may be at high risk of oral disease under CPAP treatment. 226 Conversely, a population‐based case–control study conducted in France and comparing OSA patients treated with CPAP with matched non‐OSA individuals, found that oral health (defined based on plaque and calculus index, gingival inflammation index, and the number of functional masticatory units) was similar between the groups, suggesting a potentially positive effect on the oral health of OSA resolution or improvement by CPAP. 227 Indeed, CPAP was found to be effective in improving health‐related quality of life in OSA patients, and its impact on oral health deserves further investigation. 228

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: Sleep disorders represent a significant public health concern due to their impact on general health. They have been linked to cognitive impairment and have been demonstrated to elevate the risk of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes, metabolic disorders, cancer, and mortality. Sleep disorders are prevalent in the general adult population in Europe and the United States. The present article aimed to highlight the association between sleep disorders and periodontitis, a common oral disease, which has been linked to similar comorbidities.

The data reviewed indicate that there is a correlation between sleep duration and/or sleep disturbance and oral/periodontal health, as evidenced by epidemiological studies with large sample sizes. The literature supports the biological plausibility of this association in a complex and multifactorial interplay and indicates the relevance of a tailored clinical approach in line with the current scientific evidence. Despite the strength of the association that may be weak in some cases and the lack of data for a causal link, periodontitis, sleep disorders, and OSA may be frequently encountered. This should be considered also in clinical practice where specific clinical management strategies should be applied bearing in mind that these conditions have an independent impact on quality of life that may be enhanced when they occur simultaneously. Thus, oral and periodontal diseases should be screened in patients seeking medical advice and treatment for sleep disorders (e.g., MAD or CPAP), as well as sleep disorders should be screened in patients consulting a dentist, especially when they have periodontitis. It is therefore imperative to disseminate information to both patients and healthcare professionals (i.e., dentists and physicians) regarding this relationship because knowledge transfer and increased awareness are the first approaches to empowering individuals to take proactive steps in managing their diseases and promoting health.
